title: Joshua 19:17–23
context: The fourth lot falls to Issachar, whose inheritance is given mainly as a list of towns ending at the Jordan, including Jezreel and Shunem, places that later appear in Israel’s story (compare 2 Kings 4:8). The brief section shows the same orderly pattern as the other allotments: a lot, a border or list of towns, and a closing summary by families. Some of the places can be identified with reasonable confidence, while others remain uncertain. Readers in both traditions commonly treat these verses as shared ground on the gift of land, the fulfillment of God’s promise to the patriarchs, and the dignity of each tribe’s portion. The passage raises no point of division between them.

verses.text: The fourth lot came out for Issachar, even for the children of Issachar according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the fourth lot comes out for Issachar according to their families. God’s ordering of the allotment includes each tribe in turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot again as God’s chosen way of assigning inheritance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple statement of God’s orderly provision.

verses.text: Their border was to Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Jezreel and Shunem, places that later appear in Israel’s story, including Elisha’s visits to Shunem (2 Kings 4:8). The allotment sets the scene for later acts of God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence preparing places where his later works would take place. Both traditions commonly find meaning in tracing how these named towns reappear in Scripture.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see this short line of names as part of a real inheritance where families would settle. Even unfamiliar names represent homes and communities under God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as faithful record-keeping of God’s gift. The locations of Hapharaim, Shion and Anaharath are uncertain, and readers in both traditions commonly avoid speculation about them.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the list continues with Rabbith, Kishion and Ebez, filling out Issachar’s inheritance. Each name is a reminder that God’s promise was fulfilled in detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continued listing as testimony to the thoroughness of God’s provision. Readers in both traditions commonly treat these verses as shared ground on the faithfulness of God.

verses.text: Remeth, Engannim, En Haddah, and Beth Pazzez.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the towns of Remeth, Engannim, En Haddah and Beth Pazzez as further evidence of God’s generous gift. The land was not given in vague terms but in named places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the specific towns as part of the covenant inheritance. Both traditions commonly read such lists as reminders that God’s promises are concrete, while holding identifications cautiously.

verses.text: The border reached to Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth Shemesh. Their border ended at the Jordan: sixteen cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the border reaches Tabor and ends at the Jordan, enclosing sixteen cities with their villages. Issachar’s inheritance is defined and complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary count as confirming the completeness of God’s gift. Readers in both traditions commonly note that this Beth Shemesh appears to be distinct from towns of the same name elsewhere, while holding that judgment cautiously.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Issachar according to their families, the cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the closing formula as affirming Issachar’s inheritance by families. The pattern of the allotments emphasizes that every household mattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated summary as underlining God’s faithfulness to each tribe. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple conclusion to the allotment.
